title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
interviewTips: Clarify input: can root be null? Should you return [] vs null? What is expected node value range?
Trade-off: BFS with queue is iterative O(n) and most intuitive; DFS with depth index also O(n) but uses call stack - discuss recursion depth risk on skewed tree (stack overflow in C++/Java).
Edge-case tip: capture level size before loop (int n = q.size()) - otherwise mixing next level nodes corrupts grouping; always check null children before enqueue.
Follow-up readiness: be ready to extend to Zigzag (103), Bottom-up (107), Right-side view (199) - all reuse same level-separation template.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Height + Collect Level by Level
approaches.intuition: If we knew tree height h, level order is just collect all nodes at distance 0, then distance 1, ..., distance h-1 from root. Distance-k nodes can be found by simple recursion: go down k steps.
approaches.theory: First compute height via max(leftHeight, rightHeight)+1. Then for each level i in [0,h), run a DFS that decrements level until 0 and appends node.val. This repeats full traversals h times. Correct because collect(root,i) visits exactly nodes whose depth==i in left-to-right order. Time is O(n*h) since each of h levels scans O(n) nodes. In worst skewed case h=n => O(n^2); in balanced case h=log n => O(n log n). Space is O(h) recursion stack for height/collect plus O(n) output.

timeComplexity.explanation: h = height. Each of h levels does a full O(n) traversal to find nodes at that depth. Worst O(n^2) for skewed chain (h=n), O(n log n) for balanced tree.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Recursion stack depth h for height/collect, plus O(n) for output (not counted as auxiliary by some interviewers). No queue used.

edgeCases: Skewed chain e.g. [1,null,2,null,3] => [[1],[2],[3]] with O(n^2) time - highlights inefficiency
Unbalanced with missing children - null checks prevent crash

approaches.name: Approach 2: BFS with Queue and Level Size
approaches.intuition: Process tree level by level using a FIFO queue. All nodes of current depth are in queue; snapshot queue size, pop exactly that many, push their children for next level.
approaches.theory: BFS guarantees visitation in increasing depth order because queue is FIFO: nodes enqueued earlier (shallower) are dequeued earlier. By fixing n = q.size() at start of each while iteration, we isolate one level. Each node is enqueued and dequeued exactly once, preserving left-to-right order by pushing left before right. This yields correct level grouping in single pass.

timeComplexity.explanation: Each of n nodes enqueued and dequeued once, O(1) work per node.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Queue holds at most one full level (max width). Worst O(n/2)=O(n) for perfect tree last level; plus O(n) output.

steps: n=2, pop 9 (no children), pop 20 (push 15,7) => level [9,20], q=[15,7]

edgeCases: Skewed tree => queue size stays 1, still O(n)
Large width (perfect tree) => queue grows to ~n/2, fits in memory O(n)
